title: Should university be free?

turns.speaker: Ruby
turns.text: The manifesto has free tuition in it again. No fees, funded from general taxation.

turns.speaker: Kwame
turns.text: Which sounds progressive and mostly isn't, and that's the bit that always gets skipped.

turns.speaker: Kwame
turns.text: Graduates earn more than average. Funding them from everyone's taxes means a warehouse worker pays for a dentist's training.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: That holds if the tax system is flat. It isn't, so the dentist pays more of it back anyway.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: The stronger case for me is what fees do to choices. People pick subjects by expected salary rather than by what they're good at, and that's a real cost you don't see on any balance sheet.

turns.speaker: Ruby
turns.text: Scotland's free and the participation gap between rich and poor didn't close, though. That's the finding that stopped me.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Because the barrier was never the tuition. It's living costs and school attainment at sixteen.

turns.speaker: Elena
turns.text: Abolishing fees without maintenance grants helps the people who were coming anyway.

turns.speaker: Kwame
turns.text: So we agree the money should go somewhere, we just disagree about where.

turns.speaker: Ruby
turns.text: Grants over fees, then. Which is much less popular as a slogan.

points: A manifesto proposes abolishing tuition fees, funded from general taxation.
Kwame argues this is less progressive than it sounds, since graduates earn above average and non-graduates would fund them.
Elena counters that progressive taxation recovers some of this, though Kwame says not most.
Elena's stronger argument is that fees distort subject choice towards expected salary.
Ruby cites Scotland, where free tuition did not close the participation gap between rich and poor.
Elena explains that the real barriers are living costs and attainment at sixteen, so maintenance grants matter more than abolishing fees.
